title: Sandalwood and castor
hook: You are sandalwood and I the poor castor plant beside You, made fragrant by Your nearness (Asa, Ravidas, ang 486)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Begampura, Ravidas's city with no sorrow, no fear, and no second or third. Your line was the city without sorrow. Whose weight did you lift? Day seven hundred seventy-six.

Sandalwood is prized for its scent, and its fragrance can linger on whatever it touches. The castor plant is a scrappy, weedy shrub that springs up along roadsides and in waste ground. Nobody plants a castor bush for its smell. Yesterday Ravidas built a whole city in song, a place without sorrow. Today he turns from the city to himself, and he reaches for these two plants. He puts them side by side in a hymn, and he knows exactly which one he is. Today: sandalwood and castor.
screen: `SANDALWOOD, PRIZED FOR ITS SCENT.` → `CASTOR, A ROADSIDE WEED.` → `RAVIDAS KNOWS WHICH HE IS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 486. In paraphrase, Ravidas sings to the Lord: You are sandalwood, and I am the poor castor plant, living close beside You. From a lowly tree I've become a lofty one, for Your sweet fragrance has come to dwell in me. Hear how the change happens. The castor doesn't turn into sandalwood. It doesn't train or strive its way to a better scent. It just grows near, and the fragrance moves across the gap and settles in. That's the whole picture. Nearness does the work. Here's the second turn. Ravidas keeps going with more pairs. In paraphrase: You are silk, white and yellow, and I am a poor worm. And then the refrain: Madho, I seek the shelter of the company of Your holy ones; I'm full of faults, and You are generous. The company of the holy ones, in Sikh words sangat, is where the nearness happens. It's not only the Lord far above. It's the people you stand beside. A gathering where the Name is sung can rub off on whoever sits in it. And the third turn is about Ravidas himself. This is the leather-worker from two days ago, whose people some refused to touch. In this hymn he doesn't deny that he feels low. He says it plainly. But he doesn't stay there. A low plant beside sandalwood, he says, comes away smelling of something else. Not by changing what it is, but by where it chose to stand. Made fragrant.
screen: `YOU ARE SANDALWOOD, I THE CASTOR.` · `NEARNESS DOES THE WORK.` · `SILK AND A WORM; THE HOLY COMPANY.` · `NOT BY CHANGING, BUT BY STANDING NEAR.` · then, large: `MADE FRAGRANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand near someone good. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose goodness you can almost smell: the kind one, the patient one, the one who leaves a room lighter than they found it. Picture yourself standing beside them for a minute. Don't try to be like them. Just be near, and let something of them settle on you. Then think of one way to spend time near them, or near a gathering like that, this week. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Chandan. Sandalwood, Ravidas's picture for the Lord: a weedy castor plant growing beside it comes away made fragrant, just by standing close.
Your line: made fragrant. Today, choose where you stand: one conversation, one meal, one hour near someone whose goodness rubs off. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Ravidas's sandalwood hymn is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs often use its picture to speak of the sangat, the holy company, whose nearness shapes the one who joins it.
